title: AI for Real Estate Agents: Use It for the Blank Page, Not the Message
summary: Where AI saves real estate agents real time, where it costs you trust, and a simple rule for client messages: AI drafts, you write what gets sent.
body_markdown:
Every real estate tool now has AI in it. The CRM drafts your follow-ups, the website writes your blog, and there's a button that will text your whole sphere "Happy Fall!" in your voice.


Some of that is worth having. Some of it chips away at the reason people refer you.


A Chicago brokerage leader drew the line clearly while evaluating CRMs for their agents. "We love AI. AI is great. There's a place for it," they told us. "But we don't need it crafting messages for people." If it helps with the blank page, fine. But they want the parts a machine smooths out: "I want the weird exclamation marks. I want the human side of the communication."


That's a good rule for any agent whose business comes from people who know them. Here's how to apply it, task by task.


**Fast facts:**


-


AI is strongest on work clients never see: research, summaries, first drafts, data cleanup.


-


It's weakest on messages to people who know you. They can tell, and it reads as a form letter.


-


You're responsible for anything AI writes in your marketing, including fair housing language and listing facts.


-


Never paste a client's private details into a public AI tool without checking your brokerage's policy.


-


A good test: if the client would feel differently knowing a bot wrote it, write it yourself.


*Image: An AI assistant answering a question about your own contacts and notes*


## Use it, draft with it, or do it yourself


Here's how we'd sort the common jobs.


Task


Verdict


Why


Research a neighborhood or a seller before a listing appointment


Use AI


Fast background, and you check it before you use it


Summarize your notes from a showing or a long call


Use AI


Saves time, nobody else sees it


Sort and tag a messy contact list


Use AI


Tedious work with low risk, as long as you review it


First draft of a listing description


Draft with AI


Gets you past the blank page; you fix facts and tone


Outline for a market update or blog post


Draft with AI


Structure is easy to automate; local insight isn't


Ideas for what to say to someone you haven't talked to in a while


Draft with AI


Prompts based on your notes can jog your memory


Texts to past clients and friends


Do it yourself


These people know your voice


Replies during a negotiation


Do it yourself


Tone and timing matter, and the stakes are high


Condolence, congratulations, thank-you notes


Do it yourself


A generic note here does more harm than no note


The pattern: the closer the words get to a person who trusts you, the less AI should touch them.


## Why AI messages backfire with your sphere


A new lead from a portal doesn't know how you write. An auto-reply that's quick and polite is fine.


Your past clients do know. They've read your texts at 10 p.m. during inspection week. When "Hope you're settling in well! Let me know if there's anything I can do!" arrives in a voice that sounds like every other agent's, they notice, even if they couldn't say why. It reads as a mass mailing, because it is one.


Referral businesses run on the opposite feeling: that you were thinking about them specifically. One short, slightly messy text about something you actually remember ("Did the twins make the travel team?") beats a perfect paragraph from a template.


## Where AI does help an agent


Before an appointment, ask an AI assistant to summarize recent sales on a street, the history of a subdivision or what a seller's company does. Check anything you'll repeat to a client against the MLS or public records.


After a conversation, dictate notes in the car, then have AI clean them into a few lines on the contact: what they want, the timeline, the kids' names. That's the kind of detail that makes your next real text better.


Your database is another good fit. Grouping 1,500 contacts into past clients, lenders, neighbors and investors by hand takes days. AI connected to your contacts can propose groups in minutes for you to review.


Listing descriptions, open house posts and market update outlines are fine places to start with AI too, as long as you rewrite them.


## Prompts that work


Specific prompts get better first drafts. A few to try:


-


"Draft a 120-word listing description for a 1962 brick ranch with a new roof and original hardwood floors. Describe the home, not the buyer. No exclamation points."


-


"Here are my notes from a call with a past client. Pull out anything I should follow up on and when."


-


"Give me three questions to ask a seller who inherited a house and lives out of state."


-


"Group these contacts by how I know them, based on the notes. Flag anyone you're unsure about."


Notice what's not on the list: "Write a text to my past client checking in." That one's yours.


## Fair housing and accuracy: you're still the author


AI tools learn from a lot of real estate copy, and some of it describes the buyer instead of the home. Phrases like "perfect for a young family" or "ideal for empty nesters" can raise fair housing problems under the Fair Housing Act, which bars ads that show a preference based on familial status and other protected classes. Ask for descriptions of the property, and read every draft for words about people.


Facts are the other risk. AI will confidently invent a school district, a square footage or a lot size. The listing goes out under your license, so check every number against the MLS and the documents.


And watch what you paste in. Contracts, financial details and client phone numbers don't belong in a public chatbot. Check your brokerage's policy on AI tools before you share anything confidential.

## Who this isn't for


If you run a team handling hundreds of online leads a month, automated first replies may be worth it. Speed matters with strangers who filled out a form five minutes ago. Use AI there, and keep it away from your sphere.


And if you love writing every listing description from scratch, keep doing it. Nothing here says you have to use AI at all.


## FAQ


### How can real estate agents use AI?


For research before appointments, summarizing notes, organizing contacts, and first drafts of listing descriptions and marketing. Keep it out of personal messages to clients and people who know you.


### Should realtors use ChatGPT to write texts to clients?


For new leads, a quick AI-assisted reply can be fine. For past clients and your sphere, write texts yourself. They know your voice, and a generic message reads like a mass mailing.


### Is it legal to use AI for listing descriptions?


Yes, but you're responsible for what's published. Check every fact against the MLS, and remove language that describes the ideal buyer rather than the property, since that can raise fair housing issues.


### What AI tools do real estate agents use?


General assistants like ChatGPT and Claude, AI features inside CRMs and listing platforms, and transcription tools for notes. The tool matters less than which tasks you give it.


### Can AI help me keep in touch with past clients?


It can remind you who's due and suggest what to talk about based on your notes. The message itself should still come from you.


### Is it safe to put client information into AI tools?


Be careful. Don't paste contracts, financial details or private contact information into public AI tools, and check your brokerage's policy first.


## The bottom line


AI is a good assistant and a bad ghostwriter for a relationship business. Let it do the research, the summaries, the sorting and the first drafts. Then put it down and write the message yourself, exclamation marks and all.
